lesson.menu_desc: Should, ought to and had better, and the one that is really a warning -- 37 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 10 -- What Would You Do?
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Janderson Roberto Teixeira | Lesson 10 -- What Would You Do?
lesson.grammar_point: should, ought to and had better for advice

listenings.text: Three rules for giving advice, and the first one will save you the most time. Rule one: ask what they have already decided. Most people have decided, and what they want from you is permission, so the question that actually helps is not what should I do, it is what are you tempted to do. Rule two: never say you have to. Nobody has to do anything, and the phrase makes people defend the option you are arguing against. Rule three, and this is the one that changes conversations. Say what you would do, not what they should do. It is exactly the same advice, it costs the same number of words, and it is far easier to hear, because it leaves the decision where it belongs.

Hi, sorry to call so late. I need a second opinion and you are the only person who will tell me the truth. They want me to sign on Friday. I could sign, or I could ask for two more weeks to look at the numbers properly. My worry is that if I ask for more time they will think I am not serious and go to somebody else, and honestly that may not even be true, it may just be me. So here is what I want from you. Do not tell me what I should do. Tell me what you would do, in my position, on Friday morning. Call me back whenever.

extra_audio.text: Julia says she has to decide by Friday and keeps changing her mind. Janderson asks for the two options. She explains that she can take a job in Lisbon or stay another year. He says he would ask what changes in a year. She asks whether he would not play it safe, and he asks what she is tempted to do.

paras: People almost never want advice. They want permission. Somebody describes two options, asks what you would do, and if you listen carefully you can usually hear which one they have already chosen, because they describe it second and they describe it for longer.

That does not make advice useless. It makes the strength of it matter. You should ask for a receipt is an opinion, and it costs nothing to refuse. You ought to think twice before signing is heavier and slightly more formal. You had better call him before six is a warning, and there is a consequence sitting behind it that nobody says out loud.

The mistake most people make in a second language is reaching for the strongest form because it feels clearer. It is not clearer. It is louder, and in a language you do not fully control, loud sounds like anger. The soft forms are not weaker. They are the ones people actually follow.

There is one sentence that does more work than all the modal verbs together, and it is not grammar at all: if I were you, I would. It is the same advice with the edge taken off. Nobody feels judged, nobody has to defend anything, and the decision stays where it started.
reading.source: Article -- a column on conversation in a language magazine

choices: You should not give advice unless somebody asks for it twice
